question: When a machine takes over a craft, as computers did for typesetters, does that mean the craft's workers disappear, or does the work change hands, and which of those is happening to graphic designers now that AI makes the first drafts?

issues.note: The -17% job-posts card is followed straight by the title card 'The Hand That Drew It / Episode 6'. The film opens with the statistic and then re-opens with a title, and the narration 'seventeen percent' is left hanging. The same data card reappears at R12.1 as a separate beat.

The cut goes from the dark typesetting room with the BLS 'extinction' quote to a bright 1975 office with a computer on a desk. The jump in setting and in year has no bridge. The 1975 caption is also clipped to the lower corner.

The cut goes from the paste-up page diagram to the composing-room hall with the caption 'composing room workers, 1988', which fades in faintly. The caption barely reads, and the number it introduces (86,000) is not shown at the cut.

The narration says the work did not vanish while the picture shows the same empty dark hall and then the type case, with no sign that the work continued. The line 'But the work did not vanish' has no matching image.

The cut goes from the designer at the glowing screen with poster walls to a blank dark frame with a faint caption, and the walls rebuild. The narration, 'Can the BLS see a change', is a question and the picture gives it no answer. The caption is nearly unreadable.

The cut goes from the wall of posters and a quote on projections to the chart, with a sudden switch to the cream bar-chart card. The chart is a new, cleaner look than the dark scenes around it. It then jumps to the job-post corkboard with no linking line in the narration.
'Outside the forecasts, one...' cuts from the designer scene to the dark composing room, which repeats the 1988 imagery. The picture does not match the narration, which is about freelance demand.
The cut goes from the poster walls and the freelancer line to the composing room, with the caption 'the comparison, with a caution' fading in over a picture unrelated to a comparison.

The cut goes from the type case and the designer wall with 'no projection can settle it yet' to a dark street with no figure, an unlit shop and nothing to say. The ending is abrupt and lacks a closing image tied to the question.
The corkboard of job posts runs through R10.3 to R10.8 with only the captions changing.
The same sepia photo of a man with a pipe runs across R03.8 and R04.1-R04.2, with little new to look at.
Three quote and chart cards run in a row: the 'newest projections' quote card (R08.1-R08.4) and the graphic designers chart (R08.5-R08.8). Only text changes.
The type case is shown again and again, in R11.1-R11.2, R11.4, R11.6 and R11.7, in near-identical frames, in the recap.
The corkboard of cards is shown twice, in R00.4 and R00.5, and again in R10.3-R10.8 and R12.3-R12.4, in near-identical frames.
